about: Every setting of a project's file (hive/project.json in the project's own repository, on the branch it publishes), as tools/hive/hive.py reads it: one entry for each, and no other. 'required': the file must give it; otherwise 'default' is what the hive takes when the file says nothing. 'least' and 'most' are bounds the hive enforces when it loads the file (a file outside them does not load); a setting without them is not bounded there; 'joint_bounds' are bounds on several settings together. 'fixed': the one value the hive takes. 'read_by': registry, for a mark the hive itself does not read. A key of the file, of its limits, of its members or of its judge that this list does not hold stops the file. A test of the hive (tools/hive/test_hive.py, TestTheSettingsList) holds this list to the code: neither changes alone.

presets.about: Recommended values for three ways of opening a project, whatever its judge. They are recommendations: a project's lead may change any of them, within the bounds. A setting that names no value for a way of opening keeps its default. A value written {"ask": ..., "accounts": ...} is a list of GitHub account numbers that only the lead can give ('one': exactly one; 'some': one or more). Guardians are not part of a preset: a project names them where its judge gives a figure they may waive (guardians.accounts), and members.per_guardian then has its own recommendations.
presets.trial: One account, the project lead's own, to try the whole pipeline: no wait, many deals a day.
presets.invitation: A pilot: the accounts the lead names, the hive's ordinary pace.
presets.open: Open to any GitHub account old enough, at the hive's ordinary pace.

types.protocol: the version of the hive's protocol, a whole number
types.branch: a branch's own name, with no refs/ or heads/ in front
types.path: a path in the project's repository
types.accounts: a list of GitHub account numbers
types.accounts or none: a list of GitHub account numbers, or null
types.accounts and logins: a list of GitHub account numbers; a login is taken too
types.models: a list of model identifiers (letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores, no space)
types.judge kind: one of the kinds of judge the hive holds: common, reference, relay
types.commits: a list of full commit ids
types.figures: a list of names of the judge's figures
types.conditions: a list of conditions on kept figures: {name, min or max, and optionally and: [conditions]}
types.floors: names of the judge's kept figures, each with a number
types.waivers: figures, each with the most a guardian's ruling may let it reach
types.trusted accounts: a list of entries, each {account: a GitHub account number, roles: a list of the roles the hive knows}
types.patterns: a list of paths or path patterns (dir/** for everything below a folder): printable, relative, with no empty or dot part
types.needs: a list of entries, each {kind: program, file, document or resources, and the fields of its kind}

settings.what: The version of the hive's protocol the file is written for. A file that names another does not load.
The project's name in the hive: lower-case letters, digits and hyphens. It names the project in its plan, its feed, its page and the commits of its state.
The GitHub repository the hive reads and writes for this project: the one that holds this file. A file that names another does not load, at any step of the hive or any command of a worker.

The branch the hive writes: what its judge accepted, one commit per task. Never the branch the project publishes, nor hive-state, which holds the hive's state: a file that names one branch for both, or that one, does not load.

The branch people take the project from: the repository's default branch, where this file and the tasks are read (a file that names another branch, or hive-state, does not load). The hive never writes it: the project's maintainers move it to what they have read.
Where the project's tasks are listed: one place, beside this file, read at the same commit.
The project's own quick check: one command line a worker runs in the project's sandbox before it submits. Empty: the project has none.
True stops every step of the hive for this project: nothing is read, dealt, judged or written.
A mark the hive itself does not read: the registry's own test holds that a project whose file does not say it is in service is paused, or open by invitation.

Null: any account that meets the other rules may work. A list: only these accounts, by GitHub account number (a number survives a change of login). A file that names one account alone is a trial: it may ask no wait, and its one account, named guardian too, may admit a commit of its own.
How old a GitHub account must be for the hive to read its fork as a member's: accounts made for the occasion wait.

Accounts whose forks the hive does not read, and whose work no guardian's ruling brings in. Ban by number: a number is the same everywhere, and a login can change hands. An account the file bans by number is never one of its guardians, nor trusted with a role: a file that names it both does not load. An account banned by a login and named guardian, or trusted with a role, by its number is read for its rulings or its duties, and for nothing else.
Whether the hive follows, when its rules lose nothing by it, the part of the project a member's worker says it prefers.
The models the project keeps statistics for; a worker that declares another is recorded as undeclared.

The accounts the project trusts, by GitHub account number, each once, one at least; never one the file bans by number. A guardian decides alone and at once, in public, on one named commit; it holds no key. A project names guardians where its judge gives a figure it requires by a single maximum (judge.metrics and judge.require), together with what they may waive (guardians.waive); or it names neither, and takes no ruling.

The figures a guardian may let go for one commit, and how far, one at least: only a figure the project keeps and requires by a single maximum, with a bound that is that maximum at least. The commit is judged again in full, that figure aside. Given together with guardians.accounts, or not at all.

How many active members one guardian covers. Beyond guardians times this number, the hive deals no task to a new member; those that are active go on. Null: no such bound. A file that sets it without naming a guardian does not load; where a project names guardians, the recommendations are its own (not those of a trial, which has one account).
A member is active while it holds a task, and for this many days after each candidate of its own that the project accepted.

The accounts the project trusts with a role, by GitHub account number, each once, with their roles: cut, the project's cutting, is the one role there is, and a file that names another does not load. Never one the file bans by number; one it bans by a login is still read for its duties. Such an account asks for a duty of its role in its own fork (hive.py duty), and the hive deals one duty of a role at a time, to the least loaded account that asked; a duty is counted apart from everything the account does as a member. A cut duty ends on its proposal (a commit at hive/cut in the account's fork), which the run holds to the cutter's gate and records, and publishes nothing; or it runs out, or is given back.

The least time between two cut duties, from the moment the latest was dealt, while the project has as many tasks left to do as its cutter aims at (cutter.open). With fewer, a cut duty is dealt as soon as none is live, unless the latest ended on a cut that stands or on nothing to cut: then this time all the same.
Over how many days the duties an account was dealt are counted: of the trusted accounts that ask, the one dealt the fewest duties of the role in that time is dealt first, then a draw decides.
How long a member has to push its candidate once a task is dealt to it.
How long after that the hive still waits before the deal runs out. The same grace follows a duty's time (duty_hours).

The wait after a deal that ended without an accepted candidate: this wait, each time, after a candidate the judge examined and refused; after a deal left without a candidate or a candidate refused before the judge, this wait doubled at each such deal in a row, seven days at most. A candidate short of a proof alone costs none, nor does an ending of the hive's or the project's doing; an acceptance clears it. An hour at least; none at all (0) only while the file names one account alone as its members. A trusted account's duties have a wait of their own by the same hours (trusted.accounts).
How long a trusted account has to do a duty once it is dealt (trusted.accounts); the project's grace follows, as for a deal.
How many tasks an account may be dealt in a day, those whose candidate was accepted left out.
The most lines a candidate may change.

The most files a candidate may change. With limits.file_bytes, it bounds what all of a candidate's files weigh together (joint_bounds): its most is reached only with limits.file_bytes at 268435 bytes or less.

The largest file a candidate may leave changed, or bring in any of its own commits. With limits.files, it bounds what all of a candidate's files weigh together (joint_bounds): its most is reached only with limits.files at 16 or fewer.
The longest line a candidate may add.
The most commits a candidate may add to the project's history.
What a candidate's own commits may weigh together, as git packs them on the project's tip. One fetch of a fork writes four times this at most.
How many new branch tips of one fork the hive reads in a run; a fork with more is not read until it has fewer.
How many candidates one run judges; the others wait for the next, oldest deal first.
How long a run spends reading forks; those it has not reached wait for the next run.
How long a run spends judging: no judgement is started that could end after it.
How many candidates a plan lists at most.

How a candidate is found right. common: outputs identical to the base, and measures taken beside it (a faster or smaller same thing). reference: the unit a task names answers exactly as the project's reference does (a port, a rewrite). relay: the program is run in two phases, the second with the first's message alone, and gives the project's data back; the message's bytes and the built program's are counted (a compressor and its decompressor).
common judge: how many times each measure is taken.
The longest one judgement may take.
common judge: options handed to the project's own plug-in; a task may add its own.
Commits of the project's own history its judge reads by id (a corpus as the project had it, for instance): full ids, sixteen at most.
The judge's figures the hive keeps on a verdict's line. A goal, a requirement, a proof or a waiver can only name one of these.
The judge's proofs the project takes: kept figures named sure_<measure>, those the judged program cannot bear upon. Every goal on a figure must hold one.
What the project requires of every contribution, whatever its task: conditions on kept figures. They can only refuse.
The least a task's goal may ask of a figure, for the figures the project names: the cutter's gate (hive.py cut-check) refuses a new task whose goal asks less. No run reads it.
The most task lines one cut adds or closes: the cutter's gate refuses a larger cut. No run reads it.

How many open tasks the project's cutter aims at: below it, the cutter cuts more (docs/cutter.md). A run reads it for one thing: with fewer tasks left to do than this, a cut duty is dealt as soon as none is live (trusted.cut_hours).
The longest context a new task may carry: the cutter's gate refuses a longer one. No run reads it.

Paths no candidate may change, beside those the hive protects in every project ('always': the hive's own folder at the root, and, at any depth and in any letter case, the names and folders that steer git, CI and editors, and that coding agents read as instructions). The project's own sandbox, judge and tests are not among them: a project's file lists them here.

What a worker's machine needs for the project, which a worker's tool checks before it asks for a task and before it starts one (none: a worker's machine is not checked before an ask). A program of the system (/usr/bin/<name>, the package that provides it, and a dotted prefix of its version); a file or a document the tool fetches over https, held to its SHA-256 and size, into a folder of its own outside the clone, shown to the sandbox read-only at /needs and never run on the machine, each with the licence its owner accepts before the yes; the machine's processors, memory, free disk and architecture. No entry is ever a command, an address other than https, a file without its fingerprint, a key, an account or a service: a file that names one does not load. Not a task's needs (the tasks done first), which the tasks file gives.

joint_bounds.what: What all the files one candidate leaves changed may weigh together: limits.files times limits.file_bytes, 256 MiB at most. Each is read whole in the judging step and again in the writing step, and the merged tree is written out for the judge.

What all the files and documents of a project's needs may weigh together: 2 GiB at most. A worker's tool fetches them into a folder of its own and reads them all again, at each command that checks them.

not_settings: Where project code runs (the project's sandbox, the judge's containers, without network) is the hive's, the same for every project: no project file changes it; a project's needs add to the sandbox only one read-only folder of files held to their fingerprints (/needs), and nothing to the judge's containers.
What a member may write (branches of its own fork, nothing else) and what the hive keeps of a fork's text (nothing) are the hive's.
The hive's own code is Bee-ruche/hive's, at the commit the project's workflow names: a project's file names a kind of judge, never brings one.
What is protected in every project (the 'always' of the protected setting): a project's file adds paths to these; it removes none.

The hive's own counts: three failures that are a candidate's own before it is refused, six runs without an answer before a deal is closed at no cost, a day for a fork that could not be read, a wait that doubles up to seven days.

The hive's own bounds on what a run does besides a project's limits, which have bounds of their own: the branches it lists of one fork, what all the fetches of a run leave, what a plan carries to the other steps, how long it weighs candidates.
A project's tasks are a file of their own (hive/tasks.jsonl); a task says its files, its tier, its goal and its options there, not in the project's file.
